title: GRAIN: Molecules Are Not the Right Granularity -- Active-Ingredient Modeling for Safe Medication Recommendation
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code available at [URL]
summary:
Medication recommendation from electronic health records must balance predictive accuracy against the risk of adverse drug-drug interactions (DDIs) under polypharmacy. Existing safety-aware recommenders operate at one of two granularities: the drug code, which treats each medication as an indivisible token, or the molecular substructure, which is finer than pharmacological interaction knowledge is actually organized. We argue that the active ingredient is the missing granularity, and introduce GRAIN, a medication recommendation framework built around it.
  GRAIN encodes longitudinal patient trajectories (diagnoses, procedures, past medications) with a selective state space backbone that handles long, irregular visit sequences in linear time. On top of it we introduce a joint objective unifying three knowledge sources aligned to a common medication vocabulary: a drug-level DDI graph, an ingredient-level DDI graph obtained by normalizing medication codes to active ingredients via RxNorm, and an EHR-derived co-prescription graph. A proportional controller adapts the accuracy-safety trade-off to the observed validation DDI rate rather than fixing it a priori.
  Under strictly matched settings -- identical preprocessing, cohort, vocabulary, split, and evaluation code -- GRAIN improves over a re-implemented MambaHealth baseline on MIMIC-IV across all standard multi-label metrics (Jaccard 0.4488 to 0.4983, PRAUC 0.6911 to 0.7485, F1 0.5989 to 0.6453) while reducing the drug-level DDI rate from 0.1875 to 0.0948. We further define an ingredient-level DDI rate, a safety measure invisible to drug-code-level evaluation. The results indicate that ingredient-level normalization recovers predictive signal erased by code-level aggregation, and that it is complementary to, rather than in competition with, accurate sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: GRAIN is a medication recommendation framework built around the active ingredient as the missing granularity between drug code and molecular substructure, using a selective state space backbone with a joint objective unifying drug-level DDI, ingredient-level DDI, and co-prescription graphs, plus a proportional controller for adaptive accuracy-safety trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing safety-aware medication recommenders operate at either drug-code or molecular-substructure granularity, neither of which aligns with how pharmacological interaction knowledge is organized. The active ingredient is argued to be the missing granularity that can recover predictive signal lost by code-level aggregation.
AI.method: GRAIN encodes longitudinal patient trajectories with a selective state space backbone handling long irregular visit sequences in linear time. It introduces a joint objective unifying three knowledge sources: a drug-level DDI graph, an ingredient-level DDI graph (via RxNorm normalization), and an EHR-derived co-prescription graph. A proportional controller adapts the accuracy-safety trade-off dynamically to the observed validation DDI rate.
AI.result: Under strictly matched settings on MIMIC-IV, GRAIN improves over re-implemented MambaHealth baseline across all standard metrics (Jaccard 0.4488 to 0.4983, PRAUC 0.6911 to 0.7485, F1 0.5989 to 0.6453) while reducing drug-level DDI rate from 0.1875 to 0.0948. It also defines an ingredient-level DDI rate as a safety measure invisible to drug-code-level evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Ingredient-level normalization recovers predictive signal erased by code-level aggregation and is complementary to, rather than in competition with, accurate sequence modeling for medication recommendation.

title: LLMBDC: Language Model for Biological Domains Oriented Clustering of Gene Ontology
summary: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis is a foundational tool for translating large-scale genomic data into biological insights, but typically yields hundreds of redundant terms that obscure overarching themes. Existing summarization tools rely on fixed similarity metrics (REVIGO, GOSemSim, clusterProfiler::simplify()), gene-overlap measures (Metascape), or static hierarchy mappings (GO-slim), and therefore cannot incorporate biological context. Manual curation provides context-aware grouping but is subjective and labor-intensive. A scalable, context-aware framework is needed to cluster GO terms into interpretable higher-order biological domains. Here we present LLMBDC (Large Language Model for Biological Domains Oriented Clustering of Gene Ontology), a training-free framework that leverages zero-shot semantic reasoning of LLMs with confidence scoring to cluster GO terms into BioDomains using only ontology information at inference time. Benchmarked across Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Fragile X syndrome (FXS) against six baseline methods including SapBERT, LLMBDC achieved substantially higher precision, recall, and clustering performance. Against ground-truth annotations, LLMBDC improved ARI from 9.7% to 73.3% (AD) and from 15.7% to 66.6% (FXS) over REVIGO, with corresponding NMI gains from 59.9% to 73.4% (AD) and 66.0% to 79.5% (FXS). A Cauchy combination test further confirmed that aggregated BioDomains retained statistically significant functional signals. LLMBDC provides a scalable, reproducible, and interpretable route to context-aware, system-level interpretation of GO enrichment results while preserving biological specificity.

AI.tldr: LLMBDC is a training-free framework that uses zero-shot LLM semantic reasoning with confidence scoring to cluster GO enrichment terms into interpretable higher-order "BioDomains," dramatically outperforming existing tools like REVIGO across Alzheimer's disease and Fragile X syndrome benchmarks (e.g., 73.3% vs 9.7% ARI).
AI.motivation: Existing GO term summarization tools rely on fixed similarity metrics, gene-overlap measures, or static hierarchy mappings, and therefore cannot incorporate biological context. Manual curation provides context-awareness but is subjective and labor-intensive. A scalable, context-aware framework is needed to cluster GO terms into interpretable higher-order biological domains.
AI.method: LLMBDC leverages zero-shot semantic reasoning of large language models combined with confidence scoring to cluster GO terms into BioDomains. It uses only ontology information at inference time, requiring no training. The framework is benchmarked against six baseline methods including SapBERT across two disease datasets with ground-truth annotations.
AI.result: LLMBDC achieved substantially higher precision, recall, and clustering performance than baselines. It improved ARI from 9.7% to 73.3% (AD) and 15.7% to 66.6% (FXS) over REVIGO, with NMI gains from 59.9% to 73.4% (AD) and 66.0% to 79.5% (FXS). A Cauchy combination test confirmed aggregated BioDomains retained statistically significant functional signals.
AI.conclusion: LLMBDC provides a scalable, reproducible, and interpretable route to context-aware, system-level interpretation of GO enrichment results while preserving biological specificity, addressing a critical gap in the interpretation of large-scale genomic data.

title: Timescale disparity and the reduction of the chemical master equation: A geometric approach via the linear noise approximation
summary: The chemical master equation dictates the stochastic behavior of chemical reaction networks in small volumes that are well-mixed and homogeneous. Although the Gillespie algorithm is capable of generating exact realizations of the master equation, it is often computationally expensive, especially when the network exhibits disparate reaction rates and timescales. Consequently, model reduction techniques are frequently employed to reduce the computational demands of the stochastic simulation algorithm while preserving accurate timecourse statistics. Often, the reduction of the master equation is facilitated through the adaptation of deterministic techniques from singular perturbation theory, resulting in homologous -- yet fundamentally heuristic -- reduced master equations. Such heuristic reductions are often accurate when applied to linear reaction networks but inaccurate when applied to nonlinear reaction networks. The failure of heuristic reductions is not fully understood, and it remains unclear when and why the heuristic reduction of the master equation will succeed. In this work, we take a significant step towards bridging this divide by proving that every first-order reaction network admits an accurate heuristic reduction of its associated master equation provided a specific geometric criterion holds. We also discuss the implications of this result as it pertains to nonlinear reaction networks. Specifically, we explain, through the lens of geometric perturbation theory, why the heuristically reduced CME of the nonlinear Michaelis-Menten reaction network loses precision when substrate concentrations are moderate.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that heuristic model reductions of the chemical master equation (CME) are accurate for all first-order reaction networks when a specific geometric criterion holds, and uses geometric perturbation theory to explain why these reductions fail for nonlinear networks like the Michaelis-Menten reaction under moderate substrate concentrations.
AI.motivation: The Gillespie algorithm for simulating the chemical master equation is computationally expensive for networks with disparate reaction rates and timescales. Deterministic singular perturbation techniques are often adapted heuristically to reduce the master equation, but these heuristic reductions work well for linear networks while failing unpredictably for nonlinear ones. The reason for this failure is not understood, and there is no clear criterion for when such reductions will succeed.
AI.method: The authors develop a rigorous proof demonstrating that every first-order (linear) reaction network admits an accurate heuristic reduction of its master equation, provided a specific geometric criterion is satisfied. They then apply geometric perturbation theory to analyze why the heuristic reduction of the nonlinear Michaelis-Menten CME breaks down, particularly at moderate substrate concentrations.
AI.result: The paper proves a sufficiency theorem for accurate heuristic reduction of the CME in first-order reaction networks under a geometric criterion. It further provides a geometric-perturbation-theoretic explanation for the observed loss of precision in the heuristically reduced CME of the nonlinear Michaelis-Menten network at moderate substrate concentrations.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges the gap between heuristic practice and rigorous theory for CME model reduction in linear networks, and offers a principled geometric explanation for why heuristic reductions fail in nonlinear settings, potentially guiding future development of more reliable reduction techniques.

title: Why males compete rather than care, with an application to supplying collective goods
summary: The question of why males invest more into competition than offspring care is an age-old problem in evolutionary biology. On one hand, paternal care could increase the fraction of offspring surviving to maturity. On the other hand, competition could increase the likelihood of more paternities and thus the relative number of offspring produced. While drivers of these behaviours are often intertwined with a wide range of other constraints, here we present a simple dynamic model to investigate the benefits of these two alternative fitness-enhancing pathways. Using this framework we evaluate the sensitivity of equilibrium dynamics to changes in payoffs for male allocation to mating versus parenting. Even with strong effects of care on offspring survivorship, small competitive benefits can outweigh benefits from care. We consider an application of the model that includes men's competition for hunting reputations where big game supplies a benefit to all, and find a frequency-dependent parameter region within which, depending on initial population proportions, either strategy may outperform the other. Results demonstrate that allocation to competition gives males greater fitness than offspring care for a range of circumstances that are dependent on life-history parameters and, for the large-game hunting application, frequency dependent. The greater the collective benefit, the more individuals can be selected to supply it.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a simple dynamic model to investigate why males invest more in competition than offspring care, showing that even with strong benefits of care on offspring survival, small competitive advantages can outweigh parental care benefits, and demonstrating frequency-dependent outcomes in a big-game hunting application.
AI.motivation: To address the long-standing evolutionary puzzle of why males preferentially invest in competition over paternal care, by disentangling these two fitness-enhancing pathways through a simple dynamic modeling framework.
AI.method: A simple dynamic model is developed to evaluate male allocation to mating versus parenting, with sensitivity analysis of equilibrium dynamics to changes in payoff structures, including an application to men's competition for hunting reputations where big game benefits the group.
AI.result: Small competitive benefits can outweigh care benefits even when care strongly improves offspring survivorship. In the big-game hunting application, a frequency-dependent parameter region exists where either strategy can outperform the other depending on initial population proportions. Greater collective benefits select for more individuals to supply them.
AI.conclusion: Allocation to competition provides males greater fitness than offspring care across a range of life-history-dependent circumstances, and in the hunting scenario the outcome is frequency-dependent, with collective benefits promoting the competitive strategy.

title: Mechanistic bridges from receptors to whole-brain dynamics: mean-field reductions, validity domains, and computational trade-offs
summary: Many pharmacological and pathological mechanisms act at molecular, synaptic, or cellular scales, whereas the resulting phenomena of interest are often measured at the level of cortical populations and whole-brain recordings. This scale gap motivates reduced models that remain biologically interpretable while being tractable enough for whole-brain simulation, parameter exploration, and comparison with empirical signals. This review examines the receptor-aware whole-brain framework of Sacha et al. (2025) as a representative example of such a mechanistic reduction strategy. We reconstruct the mathematical lineage leading to this model, from the master-equation formalism of El Boustani and Destexhe (2009), through the semi-analytical transfer-function framework of Zerlaut et al. (2016), the conductance-based cortical mean-field model of Zerlaut et al. (2018), and the adaptive extension of Di Volo et al. (2019), before reaching the connectome-coupled whole-brain implementation of Sacha et al. \cite{sacha2025computational}. \textbf{We make explicit the assumptions on which this reduction rests and give deliberate space to the derivation and interpretation of the equations}, so that the whole-brain model is understood as the endpoint of an explicit chain of reductions and embeddings rather than as a black box. Going beyond a single lineage, \textbf{we situate this framework within a broader landscape of reduced-population models} and we survey the directions in which the lineage is now being extended, including heterogeneity, scientific machine-learning and data-driven surrogates. Finally, \textbf{we introduce algorithmic simulation cost and memory traffic as explicit hardware-independent benchmark dimensions}. The review therefore frames receptor-aware whole-brain modeling as a trade-off between mechanistic transparency, biological detail, predictive flexibility, and computational burden.

AI.tldr: A review that traces the mathematical lineage of the receptor-aware whole-brain model by Sacha et al. (2025) back through a chain of reduced cortical population models, makes explicit the underlying assumptions and derivations, situates the framework within the broader landscape of reduced population models, surveys ongoing extensions (heterogeneity, scientific machine-learning, data-driven surrogates), and introduces hardware-independent benchmark dimensions for algorithmic simulation cost and memory traffic.
AI.motivation: There is a scale gap between molecular/synaptic/cellular mechanisms and whole-brain/population-level measurements. This motivates biologically interpretable reduced models that remain tractable for whole-brain simulation and comparison with empirical data, but these reductions are often treated as black boxes.
AI.method: The review reconstructs the mathematical lineage from the master-equation formalism of El Boustani and Destexhe (2009), through the transfer-function framework of Zerlaut et al. (2016), the conductance-based cortical mean-field model of Zerlaut et al. (2018), the adaptive extension of Di Volo et al. (2019), to the connectome-coupled whole-brain implementation of Sacha et al. (2025). It makes the reduction assumptions explicit, situates the framework among other reduced-population models, and introduces hardware-independent benchmark dimensions for cost and memory.
AI.result: The review provides an explicit, step-by-step derivation and interpretation of the equations underlying the receptor-aware whole-brain model, positions it within a broader landscape of reduced population models, surveys extension directions (heterogeneity, scientific machine-learning, data-driven surrogates), and establishes simulation cost and memory traffic as explicit benchmark dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The receptor-aware whole-brain modeling framework should be understood as the endpoint of an explicit chain of reductions and embeddings, and framed as a trade-off between mechanistic transparency, biological detail, predictive flexibility, and computational burden.

title: Recursive Gaussian Processes and the Bayesian Brain
comment: What is your thought process? The Bayesian Recursive Gaussian process?
summary: Predictive coding offers a powerful framework for cortical computation, yet scalable implementations that respect both Bayesian exactness and neurobiological constraints remain scarce. We bridge this gap by formally connecting predictive coding to Recursive Gaussian Processes (RGPs). RGPs employ a single Gaussian process \( g(t, \cdot) \) indexed by layer index and input value, preventing the representational collapse of standard deep Gaussian processes while allowing learnable cross-layer dependence via \( r_{1g} \). We demonstrate that RGPs intrinsically implement hierarchical Bayesian inference, uncertainty propagation, and precision-weighted prediction error. Critically, we map RGP components---the shared GP, spike-and-slab variable selection, and MCMC dynamics---onto the canonical cortical microcircuit, providing a neurobiological substrate for these computations. Drawing on the free energy principle, we show that RGP inference minimizes variational free energy, formally linking Bayesian mechanics to neuronal dynamics. Our synthesis positions RGPs as both a principled computational tool and a candidate model for the brain's predictive machinery, generating testable predictions for laminar-specific dynamics and spectral asymmetries between feedforward and feedback processing.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges predictive coding and Recursive Gaussian Processes (RGPs), showing that RGPs intrinsically implement hierarchical Bayesian inference, uncertainty propagation, and precision-weighted prediction errors. The authors map RGP components onto cortical microcircuits and demonstrate via the free energy principle that RGP inference minimizes variational free energy, yielding testable predictions for laminar-specific dynamics and spectral asymmetries in the brain.
AI.motivation: Despite predictive coding being a powerful framework for cortical computation, there is a gap between scalable implementations that are both Bayesian-exact and neurobiologically plausible. The paper seeks to address the scarcity of such implementations by connecting predictive coding to Recursive Gaussian Processes.
AI.method: The paper formally connects predictive coding to Recursive Gaussian Processes (RGPs), which use a single Gaussian process indexed by layer and input value to prevent representational collapse. They map RGP components (shared GP, spike-and-slab variable selection, MCMC dynamics) onto the canonical cortical microcircuit, and use the free energy principle to show RGP inference minimizes variational free energy, linking Bayesian mechanics to neuronal dynamics.
AI.result: RGPs intrinsically implement hierarchical Bayesian inference, uncertainty propagation, and precision-weighted prediction errors. The mapping to cortical microcircuits provides a neurobiological substrate, and the free energy link formally connects Bayesian mechanics to neuronal dynamics, producing testable predictions for laminar-specific dynamics and spectral asymmetries between feedforward and feedback processing.
AI.conclusion: RGPs serve as both a principled computational tool and a candidate model for the brain's predictive machinery, offering a unified synthesis of Bayesian inference, predictive coding, and neurobiological constraints with concrete experimental predictions.

title: Bayesian comparison of Langevin dynamics for cell motility from positional observation
comment: main: 19 pages, 11 figures / SI: 14 pages, 8 figures
summary: We develop a Bayesian framework for model comparison of second-order Langevin dynamics from position-only trajectories. While approximate increment likelihoods for nonlinear position-only inference have been formulated previously, a unified evidence-based framework for comparing multiple second-order models under positional observation has remained lacking. Here we address this problem by combining exact increment likelihoods for linear Gaussian models with a previously proposed approximate likelihood for nonlinear dynamics. Synthetic-data benchmarks show reliable recovery of the generating model at fine sampling intervals and progressive loss of identifiability under coarse temporal sampling. Application to Dictyostelium discoideum trajectories demonstrates that the statistically supported model depends strongly on temporal resolution. Moreover, the selected models reproduce key statistical properties of the experimental trajectories, providing additional support for the model-comparison results. Our framework therefore offers a practical approach to evidence-based comparison of partially observed stochastic dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Bayesian framework for comparing second-order Langevin dynamics models using position-only trajectory data, combining exact increment likelihoods for linear models with approximate likelihoods for nonlinear ones. Benchmarks show reliable model recovery at fine sampling intervals, and applications to Dictyostelium discoideum trajectories reveal strong dependence of model selection on temporal resolution.
AI.motivation: A unified evidence-based framework for comparing multiple second-order stochastic dynamics models under position-only observation has been lacking, despite prior approximate increment likelihoods for nonlinear position-only inference existing.
AI.method: The framework combines exact increment likelihoods for linear Gaussian models with a previously proposed approximate likelihood for nonlinear dynamics, enabling Bayesian model comparison from position-only trajectories.
AI.result: Synthetic benchmarks show reliable recovery of the generating model at fine sampling intervals with progressive loss of identifiability under coarse sampling. Application to Dictyostelium discoideum data shows the statistically supported model depends strongly on temporal resolution, and selected models reproduce key statistical properties of the experimental trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical approach to evidence-based comparison of partially observed stochastic dynamics and demonstrates temporal resolution critically influences which model is selected.

title: A persistent random-walk model of molecular transport in neuronal dendritic trees
summary: A two-level analytical framework is presented for modeling random walk transport of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) molecules along neuronal microtubules from soma to synapses. Motivated by empirical observations of mRNA cargo motion, the transport within a dendrite is modeled by a persistent telegraph process with pauses. Theoretical expressions for the probability of traversing the dendrite and the mean time for such travel are derived for different and equal probabilities of persistence. These results are used for the construction of a semi-Markov model of motion of mRNA cargo within the whole neuron. The semi-Markov model provides the probabilities of absorption at a given synapse and corresponding mean first-passage times (MFPTs) from the soma, where mRNA is transcribed. The theoretical expressions, together with experimentally obtained parameter values, are used to calculate MFPTs for neurons with empirically reconstructed morphology. The model predicts that when retrograde persistence is stronger, the MFPT to each synapse is effectively the same. Otherwise, when the persistence is more pronounced in the anterograde direction, the transport in the neuron resembles the motion along a single dendrite -- nearly linear dependence of MFPT on the distance between soma and synapse. These findings are theoretically justified when the lengths of dendrites are considerably longer than the distance traversed during a typical run.

AI.tldr: A two-level analytical framework models mRNA transport along neuronal microtubules: a persistent telegraph process with pauses within a dendrite, and a semi-Markov model for whole-neuron transport, predicting how directional persistence biases affect mean first-passage times to synapses.
AI.motivation: To understand how mRNA molecules are transported from soma to synapses along neuronal microtubules, and how directional persistence in transport affects the distribution of arrival times at different synapses.
AI.method: A two-level analytical framework: (1) a persistent telegraph process with pauses models transport within a single dendrite, providing theoretical expressions for traversal probability and mean time; (2) these results feed into a semi-Markov model for whole-neuron mRNA cargo motion, yielding absorption probabilities at synapses and corresponding MFPTs.
AI.result: The model predicts that stronger retrograde persistence equalizes MFPTs across synapses, while stronger anterograde persistence causes transport to resemble single-dendrite motion with nearly linear MFPT dependence on soma-synapse distance. These predictions hold when dendrite lengths greatly exceed typical run distances, and are validated using experimentally derived parameters on empirically reconstructed neuronal morphology.
AI.conclusion: Directional persistence in mRNA transport is a key determinant of synaptic delivery kinetics: retrograde bias homogenizes arrival times across synapses, while anterograde bias creates distance-dependent delivery patterns in the neuron.

title: Data augmentation as a framework for modeling hippocampal contributions to generalization
comment: Accepted at Current Opinion in the Behavioral Sciences
summary: The hippocampus plays a critical role in generalization, enabling us to flexibly repurpose prior experiences to perform novel tasks. Here we suggest that data augmentation---a machine learning strategy to improve generalization by refactoring prior experience---offers a useful framework to conceptualize and model hippocampal function. We begin by outlining how data augmentation operates across two timescales: the traditional ``offline'' setting, where refactoring training data yields more general representations, and an ``online'' setting, where retrieved experiences can be flexibly refactored at test time to support zero-shot inference. We suggest that these `offline' and `online' computational strategies map onto functions supported by the hippocampus. Critically, we argue that these computational tools can be leveraged to develop formal `linking functions' between experimental evidence and theoretical claims, such that a unified modeling approach can be used to predict the diverse behaviors that depend on the hippocampus---from navigating in high-dimensional sensory environments to more abstract inferences. We hope this perspective, and the modeling strategies it makes available, will support new efforts to formalize and evaluate theories of hippocampal function.

AI.tldr: The authors propose data augmentation—a machine learning strategy for improving generalization—as a unifying framework for understanding hippocampal function across offline (training) and online (test-time) computational timescales.
AI.motivation: To provide a formal framework that bridges experimental evidence and theoretical claims about hippocampal function, enabling unified modeling predictions across diverse hippocampal-dependent behaviors.
AI.method: The paper maps data augmentation strategies (offline refactoring of training data and online flexible refactoring of retrieved experiences) onto hippocampal functions, and proposes leveraging these computational tools as formal linking functions between experiments and theory.
AI.result: The framework offers a unified modeling approach to predict hippocampal-dependent behaviors ranging from navigation in high-dimensional sensory environments to abstract inferences, and supports new efforts to formalize and evaluate hippocampal theories.
AI.conclusion: Data augmentation provides a useful conceptual and computational framework for modeling hippocampal generalization, with the potential to formalize and test theories of hippocampal function.

title: NeuroWorld: A Latent Brain World Model for Stimulus-Conditioned Human Brain Dynamics
summary: Forecasting human brain activity during naturalistic experience requires modeling how endogenous neural states evolve causally under continuous sensory drive. Existing brain encoding models instead frame this as stimulus-to-response regression without strict temporal constraints, allowing future stimuli to leak into current predictions. We introduce NeuroWorld, to our knowledge the first brain world model, which casts naturalistic brain functional dynamics prediction as stimulus-conditioned evolution in a learned latent brain-state space, separating endogenous states (measured via fMRI) from exogenous multimodal stimuli across two stages. Latent Dynamics Learning (LDL) jointly learns a transition-sufficient representation and causal dynamics through next-latent prediction, without reconstructing the observed fMRI signal. Latent Rollout Decoding (LRD) freezes LDL, autoregressively rolls latent states forward from an observed fMRI prefix, and decodes them into subject-specific whole-brain responses. Across three naturalistic movie-fMRI benchmarks spanning 30 participants, including our newly collected Singapore Multimodal Imaging & Naturalistic Dataset (SG-MIND; 20 participants, 8,519 paired stimulus-response clips, 140.7 person-hours of viewing), NeuroWorld achieves state-of-the-art multi-step rollout performance under strictly causal stimulus access, with greater robustness to long-horizon autoregressive drift, supporting reliable simulation of extended brain-state trajectories. Extensive interpretability analyses characterize the functional organization of the learned dynamics, establishing latent-space world modeling as a principled framework for causal forecasting of human brain activity.

AI.tldr: NeuroWorld is the first brain world model that forecasts human brain activity during naturalistic experience by modeling causal, stimulus-conditioned evolution of endogenous neural states in a learned latent space, achieving state-of-the-art multi-step rollout prediction on naturalistic movie-fMRI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing brain encoding models treat fMRI prediction as stimulus-to-response regression without strict temporal constraints, allowing future stimuli to leak into current predictions. This violates causal forecasting principles and fails to model how endogenous neural states evolve under continuous sensory drive. A principled framework for causal, temporally-constrained brain dynamics prediction is needed.
AI.method: NeuroWorld casts brain dynamics prediction as stimulus-conditioned latent state evolution with two stages: (1) Latent Dynamics Learning (LDL) jointly learns a transition-sufficient representation and causal dynamics via next-latent prediction without reconstructing fMRI, and (2) Latent Rollout Decoding (LRD) freezes LDL, autoregressively rolls latent states forward from an observed fMRI prefix, and decodes them into whole-brain responses. Separates endogenous fMRI states from exogenous multimodal stimuli.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art multi-step rollout performance under strictly causal stimulus access across three naturalistic movie-fMRI benchmarks spanning 30 participants, including the newly collected SG-MIND dataset (20 participants, 8,519 paired stimulus-response clips, 140.7 person-hours). Demonstrates greater robustness to long-horizon autoregressive drift, supporting reliable simulation of extended brain-state trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability analyses characterize the functional organization of learned dynamics, establishing latent-space world modeling as a principled framework for causal forecasting of human brain activity during naturalistic experience.

title: Divisive Normalization Shapes Low-Rank Slow Manifolds for Continuous Working Memory
summary: The ability to robustly maintain and update continuous variables is a hallmark of working memory. While classical continuous attractor networks suffer from severe fine-tuning fragility, standard artificial recurrent neural networks (RNNs) like GRUs and LSTMs typically fail to stably learn continuous manifolds, instead shattering the state space into discretized point attractors. To bridge this gap, we draw inspiration from divisive normalization, a canonical neural computation widely observed across cortical circuits, and propose the Recurrent Divisive Normalization Network (RDNN), a minimal and algebraically isolated model of dynamic division. Through dynamical systems analysis on canonical working memory tasks, we demonstrate that this biophysical constraint allows the network to converge to robust, high-fidelity slow manifolds. Furthermore, we analyze the gradient dynamics of divisive normalization during Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), showing that it introduces an activity-dependent local gradient scaling. This scaling dampens parameter updates in highly active regimes, which empirically aligns with a significant self-compression of the network's effective rank, confining the recurrent dynamics to a tight, low-dimensional subspace while avoiding the optimization pathologies associated with explicit low-rank factorization. Finally, ablations demonstrate that while subtractive inhibition can maintain static memories, divisive normalization is mathematically essential to prevent manifold shattering under time-varying inputs. Our findings identify divisive normalization not merely as a biological artifact, but as a critical computational mechanism for learning high-fidelity continuous representations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Recurrent Divisive Normalization Networks (RDNN), a minimal recurrent neural network incorporating divisive normalization, which learns stable continuous manifolds for working memory tasks without the fine-tuning fragility of classical continuous attractors or the discretization issues of standard RNNs.
AI.motivation: Classical continuous attractor networks are fragile to fine-tuning, while standard RNNs (GRUs/LSTMs) fail to learn stable continuous manifolds and instead shatter state space into discrete attractors. The paper seeks a middle ground by drawing on divisive normalization, a widely observed cortical computation.
AI.method: The RDNN embeds divisive normalization as a single, algebraically isolated dynamic division operation. The authors analyze its dynamics on canonical working memory tasks, study gradient dynamics during BPTT showing activity-dependent local gradient scaling, and examine its effect on effective rank and low-dimensional subspace confinement.
AI.result: RDNN converges to robust, high-fidelity slow manifolds. The gradient scaling dampens updates in highly active regimes, causing self-compression of effective rank into a low-dimensional subspace without explicit low-rank factorization pathologies. Ablations show subtractive inhibition can only maintain static memories, while divisive normalization is essential to prevent manifold shattering under time-varying inputs.
AI.conclusion: Divisive normalization is not merely a biological curiosity but a critical computational mechanism for learning high-fidelity continuous representations in working memory.

title: Phylogeny.fr: the phylogenetic platform designed for non-specialists
summary: Phylogenetic analysis has become a standard approach across many areas of biology, yet the growing complexity of phylogenetic methods and software remains a major obstacle for non-specialists. Since its launch in 2008, Phylogeny.fr has provided an accessible web platform for building phylogenetic trees using widely accepted methods without requiring local software installation. Here, we present a major redesign and modernization of the service. The new version integrates state-of-the-art tools while preserving historical programs for legacy support and relies on modern web architecture and HPC infrastructure. New interactive React-based viewers, ReSeqt and Reactree, provide intuitive exploration and publication-ready visualization of alignments and trees. The Blast-Explorer companion tool has also been updated and now includes clustering options. By combining ease of use, methodological flexibility, and modern phylogenetic tools, the new Phylogeny.fr addresses the needs of researchers, teachers, and students seeking accessible and reliable phylogenetic analyses.

AI.tldr: This paper describes a major redesign and modernization of Phylogeny.fr, a web platform for building phylogenetic trees, which now integrates state-of-the-art tools, new interactive React-based viewers (ReSeqt and Reactree), an updated Blast-Explorer with clustering options, and modern web/HPC infrastructure while preserving legacy programs.
AI.motivation: Phylogenetic analysis is widely used in biology, but the growing complexity of methods and software creates barriers for non-specialists. An accessible, user-friendly web platform that keeps pace with modern tools is needed.
AI.method: The authors redesigned and modernized the Phylogeny.fr service by integrating state-of-the-art phylogenetic tools, preserving historical programs for legacy support, adopting modern web architecture and HPC infrastructure, and developing new interactive React-based viewers (ReSeqt for alignments and Reactree for trees), along with updating Blast-Explorer to include clustering options.
AI.result: The new version of Phylogeny.fr provides intuitive exploration and publication-ready visualization of alignments and trees through ReSeqt and Reactree, modernized infrastructure, and an updated Blast-Explorer with clustering capabilities, combining ease of use with methodological flexibility.
AI.conclusion: The renewed Phylogeny.fr effectively addresses the needs of researchers, teachers, and students by offering an accessible, reliable, and modern platform for phylogenetic analysis.

title: NeuroInspector: A Local-First Environment for Inspecting and Annotating Hierarchical Neuroscience Datasets
summary: The growing scale and structural complexity of neuroscience datasets have made dataset inspection an increasingly distinct stage of the research workflow. Existing inspection workflows, however, remain fragmented, often relying on exploratory scripts, manual documentation, and repeated navigation of unfamiliar file structures before meaningful scientific analysis can begin. Here we present NeuroInspector, a lightweight, browser-based environment for inspecting HDF5 and NWB files. Using WebAssembly-based HDF5 parsing (h5wasm), NeuroInspector runs entirely client-side: files are opened directly from local disk, and the application implements no file-upload endpoint, including in its hosted deployment. The tool combines structural navigation, metadata inspection, sampled data previews, and path-level annotation into portable, fingerprinted "project packs" that preserve inspection decisions without modifying the original file. Rather than functioning as an analysis or validation platform, NeuroInspector provides a dedicated, traceable environment for the inspection stage that precedes formal analysis.

However, existing inspection workflows are fragmented, relying on exploratory scripts, manual documentation, and repeated navigation of unfamiliar file structures, which impedes progress toward meaningful scientific analysis.

title: A curvature-based criterion for harmonic circadian waveforms
summary: Experimental and theoretical studies of circadian rhythms have focused largely on the period, on mutants that alter it and on phase shifts, and this focus has driven the identification of clock genes and clarified how clocks entrain to light--dark cycles. The waveform of the oscillation itself, by contrast, has attracted little attention as an indicator of the properties of the underlying oscillator. To assess the waveform directly, we focus on whether the trajectory in the plane spanned by a variable and its time derivative possesses an inflection point, and we define an oscillation to be harmonic when no inflection point is present. Bioluminescence recordings from cyanobacteria and from the mammalian SCN were harmonic in this sense, as were most of the core clock components in mathematical models of the circadian clock. Numerical analysis of the Goodwin model, a minimal representation of the core circadian oscillator, yielded harmonic oscillation throughout. We confirmed this numerical trend semi-analytically using a piecewise-linearized Goodwin model. Because it evaluates the properties of a waveform without assuming a model structure, the approach we propose offers a new perspective on the waveform analysis of biological rhythms in general, not only circadian ones.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing circadian rhythm waveforms by examining whether the trajectory in the phase plane (variable vs. its time derivative) has an inflection point. Oscillations without inflection points are defined as "harmonic." Bioluminescence data from cyanobacteria and mammalian SCN, along with most core clock components in mathematical models, were found to be harmonic. The Goodwin model was analyzed numerically and semi-analytically (via piecewise linearization), confirming harmonic oscillation throughout.
AI.motivation: While circadian rhythm research has focused heavily on period, mutants, and phase shifts—leading to clock gene discovery and entrainment understanding—the waveform of the oscillation itself has been largely ignored as an indicator of oscillator properties. This paper aims to fill this gap by using waveform shape as a diagnostic tool for characterizing the underlying oscillator.
AI.method: The paper defines an oscillation as "harmonic" if the trajectory in the plane spanned by a variable and its time derivative lacks an inflection point. This criterion is applied to bioluminescence recordings from cyanobacteria and mammalian SCN, core clock components in mathematical models, and the Goodwin model. The Goodwin model is analyzed numerically and confirmed semi-analytically using a piecewise-linearized version.
AI.result: The bioluminescence recordings from cyanobacteria and mammalian SCN were harmonic. Most core clock components in mathematical circadian models were also harmonic. Numerical analysis of the Goodwin model showed harmonic oscillation throughout, and this was confirmed semi-analytically with a piecewise-linearized Goodwin model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed waveform-based approach evaluates oscillation properties without assuming a model structure, offering a new perspective on waveform analysis for biological rhythms in general—not limited to circadian rhythms.

title: What Carries the Signal in Pathology Foundation-Model Atlases? A Patient-Level Controlled Benchmark in Breast Cancer
comment: 40 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Supplementary Information (16 pages) included as an ancillary file. Segmentation outputs obtained under the Aignostics Research Access Programme; OpenTME data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Aignostics/OpenTME
summary:
Pathology foundation models are reported to encode molecular programmes in tissue morphology, but the evidence is usually a cohort-wide ranked gene list rather than a prediction for a held-out patient. We rebuild such an analysis with the patient as the unit of evidence and ask which pipeline component carries signal.
  Across 11 frozen backbones, four pre-specified gene programmes and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq (44 cells; GroupKFold by patient, all preprocessing fitted inside the fold), ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings predicts held-out programme scores at Spearman rho = 0.25-0.56, UNI2 strongest on all four (immune 0.556). A matched permutation null gives raw p ~ 1e-4 at 10,000 permutations for every cell; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0044.
  The signal is real but not uniformly morphological. Against competing models on the same patients and folds, embeddings beat tissue composition for ER/luminal, proliferation and immune (+0.280, +0.284, +0.479; p <= 0.003) but not basal, where compartment fractions alone reach 0.469 against the embedding's 0.493 (p = 0.77). Fifty-four interpretable cell-count features come within 0.043-0.085 on every programme.
  The geometric machinery contributes nothing measurable, and we identify why: the geodesic graph selects neighbours by Euclidean nearest-neighbour search and only reweights edges already chosen, so the topology is Euclidean by construction (Riemannian minus Euclidean = +0.0010, 95% CI [-0.0007, +0.0029]). Applied consistently the geometry is worse (-0.0117). Ridge regression beats the graph-and-metric decoder by +0.097 (CI [+0.069, +0.127]). The driver-count metric common in this literature is near-uninformative here: 91.8% of random six-gene panels recover >=5/6 drivers.

AI.tldr: A rigorous patient-level analysis of pathology foundation models shows real but modest signal for predicting gene programmes from H&E slides (Spearman rho 0.25-0.56), with UNI2 strongest. Signal is not uniformly morphological—embeddings beat tissue composition for some programmes but not basal. The geometric machinery (geodesic graph) contributes nothing measurable because it is Euclidean by construction, and ridge regression outperforms more complex decoders.
AI.motivation: Prior claims that pathology foundation models encode molecular programmes rely on cohort-wide ranked gene lists rather than held-out patient predictions. The authors rebuild the analysis with the patient as the unit of evidence to determine which pipeline component actually carries predictive signal.
AI.method: Uses 11 frozen backbones, 4 pre-specified gene programmes, and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq. Ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings with GroupKFold by patient and all preprocessing fitted inside the fold. Compares against tissue composition models, interpretable cell-count features, and geometric graph-based decoders with matched permutation nulls.
AI.result: Held-out programme predictions achieve Spearman rho 0.25-0.56 with UNI2 strongest (immune 0.556), significant at Holm-adjusted p=0.0044. Embeddings beat tissue composition for ER/luminal, proliferation, and immune but not basal. The geodesic geometric machinery adds nothing measurable (+0.0010, CI includes 0) because the graph is Euclidean by construction. Ridge regression beats graph-and-metric decoder by +0.097.
AI.conclusion: The signal from pathology foundation models for gene programmes is real but modest and variably morphological. Simple pipelines (mean pooling + ridge regression) capture most of the signal, while complex geometric machinery provides no added value. Simpler interpretable features nearly match embeddings, suggesting the field should prioritize rigorous patient-level validation and simple, well-validated pipelines.

title: A Quantum Reservoir for Neurodynamical Forecasting
comment: 7 pages (including references), 2 figures, Accepted at IEEE Quantum Week (QCE 2026) short technical paper, Applications category
summary: Forecasting neural activity from short recordings remains a fundamental challenge. Reservoir computing may offer an efficient paradigm for temporal prediction, however classical reservoirs typically underperform in small-data regimes. Here we investigate whether quantum reservoir computing (QRC) can help overcome this limitation. Building on recent advances, we introduce a quantum reservoir based on a transverse-field Ising model, combined with heterogeneous quantum measurements and polynomial ridge regression. On a standard benchmark task, results show that the quantum reservoir outperforms a classical counterpart overall, with prediction accuracy strongly dependent on reservoir parameters. We further demonstrate feasibility by running the same task on quantum hardware. To assess performance on biological signals, we evaluate QRC on simulated human electroencephalography (EEG) data with a parallel reservoir architecture. On this challenging task, the tested quantum reservoir did not match the performance of the classical one, but it produced stable, convergent predictions. This is a meaningful first step toward forecasting of biologically realistic neural data using a quantum reservoir. Overall, our findings indicate that although current quantum hardware and parallel reservoir architectures do not yet surpass classical methods on complex neural signals, QRC can be executed on near-term devices and does converge with realistic EEG-like data. This work establishes a practical baseline for future algorithmic and hardware developments aimed at clinical time-series forecasting with quantum systems.

QRC outperforms a classical reservoir on a standard benchmark task and runs on quantum hardware, but on simulated EEG data it does not match classical performance—though it produces stable, convergent predictions, establishing a practical baseline for future quantum clinical time-series forecasting.

AI.method: The authors introduce a quantum reservoir built on a transverse-field Ising model, combined with heterogeneous quantum measurements and polynomial ridge regression. They evaluate it on a standard benchmark task, on quantum hardware, and on simulated human EEG data using a parallel reservoir architecture.
AI.result: The quantum reservoir outperforms a classical counterpart on the standard benchmark task, with accuracy strongly dependent on reservoir parameters, and feasibility is demonstrated on quantum hardware. On simulated EEG data, the quantum reservoir did not match classical performance but produced stable, convergent predictions.
