This establishes a practical baseline for future algorithmic and hardware developments aimed at clinical time-series forecasting with quantum systems.

title: Dynamical principles of habituation across substrates and scales
summary: Habituation is a basic form of learning in which a system's response to repeated stimulation progressively diminishes but eventually recovers when the stimulus is withheld. Long studied in animals, it has increasingly been observed in unicellular organisms and non-living devices such as electronic circuits and neuromorphic materials, suggesting underlying dynamical principles that recur across domains. This review asks what those principles are: given qualitative constraints imposed by habituation on a system's response, what is the minimal dynamical structure that satisfies them? We formalize the classical hallmarks of habituation as behavioral constraints on input--output behavior, show that linear time-invariant systems are structurally incompatible with these constraints, and construct nonlinear motifs---linear fading-memory dynamics composed with static nonlinearities---that exhibit the hallmarks across diverse settings. We relate these motifs to models of specific biological systems and to physical and algorithmic realizations, from analog circuits to transient computation in machine learning.

AI.tldr: This review formalizes habituation as behavioral constraints on input-output systems, proves linear time-invariant systems cannot satisfy them, and constructs minimal nonlinear motifs (fading-memory dynamics plus static nonlinearities) that exhibit all hallmarks of habituation across diverse domains, from biology to neuromorphic materials.
AI.motivation: Habituation is observed across animals, unicellular organisms, and non-living systems, suggesting universal dynamical principles. The authors ask what minimal dynamical structure is required to satisfy the qualitative constraints of habituation.
AI.method: Formalize habituation hallmarks as behavioral constraints on input-output behavior; prove linear time-invariant (LTI) systems are structurally incompatible; construct nonlinear motifs by composing linear fading-memory dynamics with static nonlinearities; relate motifs to biological models and physical/algorithmic realizations.
AI.result: Linear time-invariant systems cannot exhibit habituation hallmarks; nonlinear fading-memory-with-nonlinearity motifs can satisfy all hallmarks across diverse settings, bridging biological models and engineered systems.
AI.conclusion: Habituation's underlying principles are captured by minimal nonlinear dynamical motifs, providing a unifying framework across biology, electronics, and neuromorphic materials, and offering a theoretical basis for transient computation in machine learning.

title: Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind
summary: Do frontier vision-language models present a coherent Theory-of-Mind (ToM) profile across tasks, matching the same human reference group, or does that profile fragment from one paradigm to the next? We evaluate a shared panel of nine frontier VLMs on two psychology-derived benchmarks: the Keysar Director Task (visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference) and the Frith-Happé animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric (intention attribution from pure motion). On the Director Task, without chain-of-thought, the panel makes the egocentric error on 78\% of trials like children rather than adults; variation is substantial across models, and reasoning rescues several models. On the triangles, the panel under-attributes intention: its ToM profile sits more than three times closer to the high-functioning-autistic-adult (HF-ASD) mean than to the typical-development-adult (TD) mean, while Goal-Directed and Random stay near TD. No model is nearest TD on both tasks; the model that looks adult-like on the Director Task falls on the HF-ASD side on the triangles, and the most TD-like model on the triangles is child-like on the Director Task. We report group-level descriptions, not diagnostic labels for any model.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates nine frontier vision-language models on two Theory-of-Mind benchmarks (Keysar Director Task and Frith-Happé animated triangles) and finds that no model exhibits a coherent ToM profile matching a single human reference group—the panel's performance fragments across paradigms, with models appearing adult-like on one task but child-like or HF-ASD-like on the other.
AI.motivation: To determine whether frontier VLMs display a coherent Theory-of-Mind profile across different psychological paradigms, or whether their ToM abilities fragment depending on the task, which has implications for how these models' social-cognitive capabilities should be characterized and evaluated.
AI.method: Nine frontier VLMs were evaluated on two psychology-derived benchmarks: (1) the Keysar Director Task measuring visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference, and (2) the Frith-Happé animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric for intention attribution from motion. Performance was compared against human reference groups including children, typical-development adults, and high-functioning-autistic adults.
AI.result: The panel makes egocentric errors on 78% of Director Task trials (child-like) without chain-of-thought, with substantial model variation; reasoning rescues several models. On triangles, the panel under-attributes intention, sitting more than three times closer to the HF-ASD mean than the TD mean, while Goal-Directed and Random scores remain near TD. No model is nearest to TD on both tasks—the model adult-like on the Director Task is HF-ASD-like on triangles, and the most TD-like model on triangles is child-like on the Director Task.
AI.conclusion: Frontier VLMs do not present a coherent Theory-of-Mind profile across tasks matched to any single human reference group; their ToM profile fragments across paradigms. The findings are reported as group-level descriptions rather than diagnostic labels for any individual model.

title: Gene Ontology-Guided Hierarchical Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology Images
comment: Accepted by ACM MM 2026. Code: https://github.com/NozomiMizore/MSGR
summary: Predicting spatial gene expression from histopathology images enables large-scale transcriptomic profiling without the cost of direct measurement. Existing methods decode the target gene set as a flat, unstructured vector, ignoring the inter-gene dependencies arising from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality. We propose MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner), which bridges this gap by incorporating the Gene Ontology (GO), a curated functional hierarchy of genes, as an explicit structural prior. MSGR organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree. Its GO-guided decoder then progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. Operating solely on the gene side, the GO-guided decoder serves as a seamless plug-in replacement that consistently improves existing architectures without requiring any image-side modifications. Extensive experiments on nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark provide empirical evidence for two central claims: GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against a state-of-the-art generative baseline, and the gain is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, as confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.

AI.tldr: MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner) improves spatial gene expression prediction from histopathology images by using Gene Ontology (GO) as an explicit structural prior, organizing target genes into a four-level GO tree and progressively refining predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. The GO-guided decoder is a plug-in replacement that consistently outperforms flat decoding across nine HEST-1k datasets (+0.027 over random hierarchy).
AI.motivation: Existing methods decode target gene sets as flat, unstructured vectors, ignoring inter-gene dependencies from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality.
AI.method: MSGR incorporates Gene Ontology (GO) as an explicit structural prior. It organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree, and its GO-guided decoder progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. The decoder operates solely on the gene side, serving as a plug-in replacement requiring no image-side modifications.
AI.result: On nine datasets from HEST-1k benchmark, GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, including against a state-of-the-art generative baseline. The gain is attributed to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating biological structure (GO) as a prior into gene decoding improves prediction quality, demonstrating that structural guidance matters for spatial transcriptomic prediction and that the benefit is specifically due to meaningful biological organization rather than just hierarchical design.

title: No persistent circadian oscillator at genome resolution: pseudo-coherence in gut microbiome dynamics
summary: Diurnal rhythms in the gut microbiome are commonly read as evidence of host-driven entrainment or of microbial oscillators that synchronise to a common clock. We reanalyse hourly genome-resolved (MAG-level) mouse-gut time series with diagnostics tailored to test that interpretation. At this resolution and for both animals in the dataset, the time-frequency representation carries no persistent ridge; the time-averaged spectrum is enhanced at low frequencies and depleted at intermediate frequencies; the lagged covariance is markedly time-asymmetric, with a global imbalance peak near tens of hours; and an amplitude-adjusted Fourier surrogate test identifies a weak time-averaged construction in the candidate circadian band, never as a fixed time-frequency ridge. The two functional guilds that carry the inferred non-normal amplification are identified independently by the rankings of two inferred dynamical modes (the reaction mode, into which fluctuations are transiently amplified, and the non-normal mode, which injects them), and recover the primary polysaccharide degraders of Bacteroidota and the secondary butyrate and propionate fermenters of Bacillota A without invoking any phase information. The conjunction of these signatures matches a stable but strongly non-normal stochastic regime, that is, pseudo-coherence: geometric amplification reshapes stochastic fluctuations onto a low-dimensional reaction subspace, producing intermittent synchronisation-like episodes, broken time-reversal symmetry, and emergent time-averaged characteristic scales without an underlying oscillator. We propose a falsifiable test via high-resolution clock-gene-knockout cohorts.

AI.tldr: Reanalysis of hourly mouse-gut microbiome time series shows that apparent circadian rhythms are not driven by oscillations but by non-normal stochastic dynamics (pseudo-coherence), where geometric amplification reshapes noise onto a low-dimensional reaction subspace, producing intermittent synchrony-like episodes without a true oscillator.
AI.motivation: Diurnal rhythms in the gut microbiome are typically interpreted as evidence of host-driven entrainment or synchronized microbial oscillators. The authors question this interpretation and aim to test it rigorously at genome-resolved resolution.
AI.method: The authors reanalyze hourly MAG-level mouse-gut time series using time-frequency representations, time-averaged spectra, lagged covariance analysis, and amplitude-adjusted Fourier surrogate tests. They also use rank diagnostics from two inferred dynamical modes (reaction mode and non-normal mode) to identify functional guilds without phase information.
AI.result: No persistent time-frequency ridge was found. Spectra showed low-frequency enhancement and intermediate-frequency depletion. Lagged covariance was time-asymmetric with a global imbalance peak near tens of hours. Fourier surrogate tests found only weak time-averaged construction in the candidate circadian band. The inferred non-normal amplification identified primary polysaccharide degraders (Bacteroidota) and secondary butyrate/propionate fermenters (Bacillota A) without phase information.
AI.conclusion: The observed microbiome rhythm-like signatures are consistent with a stable but strongly non-normal stochastic regime (pseudo-coherence) rather than genuine oscillators. A falsifiable test via high-resolution clock-gene-knockout cohorts is proposed.

title: Evolutionary Curriculum Learning Improves Biological Sequence Modeling
summary: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) have emerged as powerful generative models for biological sequences, with applications ranging from disease variant prediction to functional RNA design. However, standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure that organizes homologous sequences from evolutionarily close to highly divergent. We propose Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a training strategy that exploits this structure by progressively exposing the model to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from sampled anchors, following a power-law expansion schedule. Applied to two architecturally distinct VAE models and two biological domains--protein variant effect prediction with EVE and RNA family sequence generation with RfamGen--ECL improves downstream task performance across five random seeds per configuration. Mean ClinVar classification AUROC rises from 0.981 to 0.989 for p53; for PTEN, ECL attains 1.000 in every seed whereas the baseline is unstable (mean 0.905, falling as low as 0.54). For RNA, ECL raises mean covariance-model bit scores on all three families tested and exceeds its seed-matched baseline in 12 of 15 training runs, though with only three families the effect cannot be established as significant at the family level. Ablation experiments show that progressively expanding the sampled sequences by evolutionary distance outperforms fixed-size neighborhood sampling in addition to uniform random sampling. Evolutionary distance is therefore a useful inductive bias for ordering the training curriculum in biological sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a training strategy for biological VAEs that progressively exposes models to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from anchors using a power-law schedule, improving downstream task performance in protein variant effect prediction and RNA family generation across two architecturally distinct VAE models.
AI.motivation: Standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure in multiple sequence alignments that organizes homologs by evolutionary relatedness. The authors hypothesize that exploiting this structure through curriculum learning can improve model training.
AI.method: ECL progressively exposes the VAE to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from sampled anchor sequences, following a power-law expansion schedule. The method is evaluated on two architecturally distinct VAEs (EVE for protein variant effect prediction and RfamGen for RNA family sequence generation), with comparisons against fixed-size neighborhood sampling and uniform random sampling baselines.
AI.result: ECL improves mean ClinVar classification AUROC from 0.981 to 0.989 for p53, and for PTEN achieves perfect 1.000 AUROC in every seed while the baseline is unstable (mean 0.905, falling to 0.54). For RNA, ECL raises mean covariance-model bit scores on all three families tested and beats seed-matched baselines in 12 of 15 runs. Ablations show progressive expansion outperforms fixed-size neighborhood and uniform random sampling.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary distance provides a useful inductive bias for ordering the training curriculum in biological sequence modeling, though for RNA the effect could not be established as statistically significant at the family level given only three families were tested.

title: Deep Learning CNN and Recurrence Analysis for Alpha Gamma EEG Biomarkers in Fragile X Syndrome
summary: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by reduced expression of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), leading to disrupted synaptic plasticity, cortical hyperexcitability, and impaired network synchronization. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a noninvasive window into these mechanisms and consistently reveals abnormalities in alpha (8 to 12 Hz) and gamma (30 to 100 Hz) oscillations that relate to inhibitory control, sensory processing, and cognition. This paper proposes a multi representation deep learning framework for automated characterization of FXS EEG phenotypes by integrating convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and recurrence plot (RP) analysis. Band limited EEG signals are decomposed into alpha and gamma components and transformed into complementary representations, including temporal feature sequences, time frequency maps, and RP images encoding the nonlinear recurrence structure. CNN modules learn discriminative spatial-spectral and dynamical textures from image based representations, while LSTM modules model temporal modulation of oscillatory activity; a hybrid CNN LSTM architecture jointly captures spatial, temporal, and nonlinear dependencies. Subject-independent evaluation demonstrates that the hybrid model outperforms single modality baselines, with gamma features providing strong discriminative power and alpha gamma integration yielding the best overall performance. These findings support deep learning with nonlinear representations as a scalable approach for EEG biomarker development in FXS, with potential utility for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment monitoring in translational settings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-representation deep learning framework combining CNNs, LSTMs, and recurrence plot analysis to automatically characterize Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) EEG phenotypes from alpha and gamma band signals. The hybrid CNN-LSTM model integrating alpha and gamma features outperforms single-modality baselines, supporting its use for EEG biomarker development in FXS.
AI.motivation: FXS is a neurodevelopmental disorder with disrupted synaptic plasticity, cortical hyperexcitability, and impaired network synchronization. EEG reveals abnormalities in alpha and gamma oscillations related to inhibitory control and sensory processing, but automated characterization of these phenotypes remains a challenge. A scalable deep learning framework is needed for reliable FXS EEG biomarker extraction.
AI.method: The framework decomposes band-limited EEG into alpha and gamma components, transforming them into complementary representations: temporal feature sequences, time-frequency maps, and recurrence plot (RP) images. CNN modules learn spatial-spectral and dynamical textures from image representations, while LSTM modules model temporal modulation of oscillations. A hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture jointly captures spatial, temporal, and nonlinear dependencies. Subject-independent evaluation compares the hybrid model against single-modality baselines.
AI.result: The hybrid CNN-LSTM model outperforms single-modality baselines under subject-independent evaluation. Gamma features provide strong discriminative power, and integrating alpha and gamma features yields the best overall performance.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning with nonlinear representations is a scalable approach for EEG biomarker development in FXS, with potential utility for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment monitoring in translational settings.

title: Beyond Gene Reconstruction: Learning Cell Representations through Complementary Transcriptomic Views
summary: The rapid growth of single-cell transcriptomic data has enabled the development of foundation models pretrained primarily by reconstructing masked expression values. This objective encourages these models to learn gene dependencies but does not directly optimize whole-cell representations, which are essential for many downstream tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a contrastive pretraining framework that learns cell representations through complementary transcriptomic views. Since standard contrastive learning is not readily applicable to single-cell pretraining, we introduce specific adaptations along three dimensions --- co-expression-guided gene partitioning, expression-aware contrast-set construction, and competence-gated contrastive onset. Specifically, we first construct two complementary views of each cell by partitioning its genes according to their co-expression structure. Then, to prevent the model from using gene-set identity as a shortcut, we construct hard negatives by permuting expression values while keeping gene identities unchanged. Finally, we introduce a competence-aware controller to determine how the contrastive objective is applied. Experiments on cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network inference demonstrate competitive transfer under the evaluated protocols. In the six-network GRN evaluation, our method records the highest mean AUROC and AUPRC point estimates among the compared variants, while the highest-scoring variant differs across individual networks. These results establish complementary-view contrastive learning as an effective direction for single-cell pretraining beyond gene reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a contrastive pretraining framework for single-cell foundation models that learns whole-cell representations through complementary transcriptomic views, with three specific adaptations: co-expression-guided gene partitioning, expression-aware contrast-set construction, and competence-gated contrastive onset. The method shows competitive performance on cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network inference tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing single-cell foundation models are pretrained primarily through masked expression reconstruction, which learns gene dependencies but does not directly optimize whole-cell representations needed for many downstream tasks. Standard contrastive learning is not readily applicable to single-cell pretraining, motivating the need for adapted contrastive strategies.
AI.method: The framework introduces three adaptations to contrastive learning for single-cell data: (1) co-expression-guided gene partitioning to construct two complementary views of each cell, (2) expression-aware contrast-set construction using hard negatives (permuting expression values while keeping gene identities) to prevent shortcut learning via gene-set identity, and (3) a competence-gated controller to determine when/how the contrastive objective is applied.
AI.result: Experiments show competitive transfer performance on cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network (GRN) inference. In the six-network GRN evaluation, the method achieves the highest mean AUROC and AUPRC point estimates among compared variants, though the best-performing variant varies across individual networks.
AI.conclusion: Complementary-view contrastive learning is established as an effective direction for single-cell pretraining beyond gene reconstruction, providing a viable alternative or complement to masked-expression-based objectives.

title: Funnel-like protein energy landscapes emerge from functional evolution under thermal fluctuations
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, supplemantal information (3 pages, 3 figures)
summary: Proteins perform biological functions by folding into specific native structures that are stabilized by funnel-like energy landscapes shaped through evolution. We investigate whether such foldable proteins can emerge solely from selection for function, without any direct selection for foldability. Using a two-dimensional lattice protein model with four amino-acid types, we define protein function as the equilibrium probability that a prescribed local structure forming an active site is realized at environmental temperature $T$, and use this probability as the evolutionary fitness. Amino-acid sequences spanning the entire fitness range are sampled by multicanonical Monte Carlo method and their energy and free-energy landscapes are constructed from the equilibrium conformational ensemble. We find that only within an appropriate range of environmental temperatures do high-fitness sequences spontaneously acquire funnel-like energy landscapes, despite foldability never being included in the fitness definition. High-fitness sequences are furthermore supported by only a limited number of native conformations. At low temperatures, in contrast, high-fitness sequences exhibit rugged, glass-like energy landscapes and much greater structural diversity. These results suggest that foldable proteins need not be direct targets of evolution, but can emerge as a thermodynamic consequence of maintaining function under thermal fluctuations, whereby local functional constraints organize the global fold and give rise to funnel-like energy landscapes.

AI.tldr: Using a 2D lattice protein model with four amino-acid types, the authors show that foldable proteins with funnel-like energy landscapes can emerge solely from selection for function (equilibrium probability of forming an active site), without direct selection for foldability—but only within an appropriate range of environmental temperatures.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether foldable proteins can emerge purely from functional selection pressure, without any explicit evolutionary selection for foldability or funnel-like energy landscapes.
AI.method: Two-dimensional lattice protein model with four amino-acid types; fitness defined as the equilibrium probability of realizing a prescribed local active-site structure at environmental temperature T; multicanonical Monte Carlo sampling of sequences across the fitness range; construction of energy and free-energy landscapes from equilibrium conformational ensembles.
AI.result: High-fitness sequences spontaneously acquire funnel-like energy landscapes only within an appropriate temperature range, despite foldability never being in the fitness definition. High-fitness sequences are supported by only a limited number of native conformations. At low temperatures, high-fitness sequences exhibit rugged, glass-like energy landscapes with much greater structural diversity.
AI.conclusion: Foldable proteins need not be direct targets of evolution; they can emerge as a thermodynamic consequence of maintaining function under thermal fluctuations, where local functional constraints organize the global fold and give rise to funnel-like energy landscapes.

title: Smart membrane: high content in situ monitoring barrier on chip with artificial neuronal network
summary: Conventional transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) technique provides only a low-content analysis of cell-layer conditions, necessitating repeated microscopic assessments of morphology and cell-cell contacts outside the incubator for barrier-on-chip systems. This work presents a novel high-content TEER device in the form of a novel nanoporous membrane that facilitates continuous electrical measurement of cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). The ultrathin (700 nm) membrane, composed of ultra-low-stress SixNy, is monolithically integrated into wafer-level fabricated chips sealed with glass lids. Coplanar ECIS electrodes were connected to custom electronics to record impedance under sinusoidal excitation. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were seeded and continuously recorded impedance spectra were compared with bright-field and fluorescence microscopy, revealing distinct phases of monolayer formation. With one-dimensional convolutional neural network (Conv1d) and Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) trained with a small amount of Nyquist-diagrams, phases of (I) adherence, (II) outspreading, (III) confluence and (IV) barrier maturity with tight junction formation could be recognized with 95% confidence. As further proof of concept, reversible and irreversible barrier weakening using modulators PN159 and BAC was identified in this way. Our studies have demonstrated that an immediate and automatable non-invasive detection of in-vitro barrier dynamics within barrier-on-chip systems, eliminating the need for microscopy and endpoint staining. We expect this ECIS technique will find broad applications in organ-on-chip systems for in situ monitoring physiological or pathological states of tissue barrier.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel high-content TEER device using an ultrathin 700 nm nanoporous SixNy membrane monolithically integrated into wafer-level chips, enabling continuous electrical cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). Combined with a 1D convolutional neural network and Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, the system automatically recognizes four distinct phases of endothelial monolayer formation (adherence, outspreading, confluence, barrier maturity) with 95% confidence, eliminating the need for microscopy and endpoint staining in barrier-on-chip systems.
AI.motivation: Conventional TEER techniques provide only low-content analysis of cell-layer conditions, requiring repeated microscopic assessments of morphology and cell-cell contacts outside the incubator for barrier-on-chip systems, which is labor-intensive and non-continuous.
AI.method: The authors fabricated an ultrathin (700 nm) ultra-low-stress SixNy nanoporous membrane monolithically integrated into wafer-level chips with glass lids, featuring coplanar ECIS electrodes connected to custom electronics. Continuous impedance spectra were recorded under sinusoidal excitation. A combined 1D convolutional neural network (Conv1d) and Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) were trained using a small amount of Nyquist-diagrams to classify four phases of monolayer formation. Barrier modulation with PN159 and BAC was used as proof of concept.
AI.result: The system recognized four distinct phases of monolayer formation—(I) adherence, (II) outspreading, (III) confluence, and (IV) barrier maturity with tight junction formation—with 95% confidence. Reversible and irreversible barrier weakening using modulators PN159 and BAC were successfully identified, demonstrating automatable non-invasive detection without microscopy or endpoint staining.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that immediate and automatable non-invasive detection of in-vitro barrier dynamics within barrier-on-chip systems is achievable, eliminating the need for microscopy and endpoint staining. The authors expect this ECIS technique to find broad applications in organ-on-chip systems for in situ monitoring of physiological or pathological states of tissue barriers.

authors: Srinivasa Rao P Vangmayi P Reddy
title: Statistical Mechanics of Learning on Product Wasserstein Manifolds
summary: Normally the statistical mechanics of learning treats constraints on weight distributions as restrictions that shrink the space of possible solutions. Therefore, it reduces model capacity. In this paper we would like to take a contrary approach, which, however, is based on the earlier work on distribution-constrained perceptrons. Rather than treating a prescribed weight distribution as a mere restriction, we propose that it defines the intrinsic geometry upon which learning naturally unfolds. We formulate both deep neural networks and variational quantum circuits as gradient flows on a product of Wasserstein manifolds -- one classical Wasserstein space for each layer and one quantum Wasserstein space for the circuit parameters. Within this geometry, the capacity reduction, which was previously associated with distributional constraints, appears as the metric structure of the constraint manifold itself. We develop a hierarchical mean-field description for deep networks, extend the framework to the quantum setting using the quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1, and introduce two such practical algorithms, Hierarchical DisCo-SGD and Quantum DisCo, that follow approximate geodesics on the manifold of the product itself. Experiments on teacher-student problems, standard image classification tasks, and small variational quantum classifiers show that respecting these distributional geometries improves generalization, stabilizes training, and reduces the severity of barren plateaus compared with unconstrained and purely norm-based baselines. This approach firstly reframes structural constraints as geometric priors and suggests a route for incorporating biological, spectral, or hardware-derived distributional information into both learning systems, viz., classical and quantum learning.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes distributional constraints in learning from capacity-reducing restrictions to geometric priors, formulating deep neural networks and variational quantum circuits as gradient flows on product Wasserstein manifolds, and introduces Hierarchical DisCo-SGD and Quantum DisCo algorithms that follow approximate geodesics, improving generalization and reducing barren plateaus.
AI.motivation: Traditional statistical mechanics treats weight distribution constraints as restrictions that shrink solution space and reduce model capacity. The authors propose a contrary view: rather than treating prescribed weight distributions as mere restrictions, they should define the intrinsic geometry upon which learning naturally unfolds.
AI.method: Formulates deep neural networks and variational quantum circuits as gradient flows on products of Wasserstein manifolds (classical Wasserstein spaces per layer, quantum Wasserstein space for circuit parameters). Develops a hierarchical mean-field description for deep networks, extends to quantum setting via quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1, and introduces Hierarchical DisCo-SGD and Quantum DisCo algorithms that follow approximate geodesics on the product manifold.
AI.result: Experiments on teacher-student problems, standard image classification, and small variational quantum classifiers show that respecting distributional geometries improves generalization, stabilizes training, and reduces severity of barren plateaus compared to unconstrained and norm-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: This approach reframes structural constraints as geometric priors, suggesting a route for incorporating biological, spectral, or hardware-derived distributional information into both classical and quantum learning systems.

title: Interpretable MEG Decoding of Perceived Speech: Cortical Sources and the Stimulus Features That Drive Retrieval
summary:
Short segments of perceived speech can be retrieved from non-invasive magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings by deep networks trained with a CLIP-style objective against wav2vec 2.0 audio embeddings. Yet their weights do not map onto electrophysiological quantities, and it remains unclear which speech properties drive retrieval.
  We build on a high-performing MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture but redesign both its front end and decoder. Its spatial attention operates on a flattened sensor layout; we replace it with spherical harmonics defined on the three-dimensional MEG helmet geometry. We reduce the subject-specific representation from 270 to 25 branches, add a temporal filter to each branch to match it to a neuronal source in space and time, and make the convolutional decoder shallower. Ocular and cardiac components are removed before training to reduce the risk of stimulus-locked shortcuts.
  On MEG-MASC, the model reaches 39.75 +/- 0.34% Top-1 accuracy among 1005 candidates across six trained solutions, with about 20 times fewer decoder parameters. Its weights map to source space, recovering generators consistent with the speech-perception network, while left-lateralized branches carry higher-frequency rhythmic components not evident on the right. Paired MEG occlusion shows that 15 of 19 stimulus features contribute, with the largest effects for silence, sound intensity, vowels, and acoustic onsets. Random word lists behave oppositely: substituting narrative MEG into them improves retrieval, indicating that activity without narrative structure carries less recoverable information than activity during coherent speech. The wav2vec target can be reduced to about twelve learned feature dimensions without loss of accuracy, whereas strong temporal compression causes a clear loss.
  Together, source mapping and input interventions reveal what drives retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an improved MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture using spherical harmonics on the MEG helmet geometry and a reduced subject-specific representation (25 branches with temporal filters), achieving 39.75% Top-1 accuracy on MEG-MASC with ~20x fewer decoder parameters. The model's weights map to source space, revealing left-lateralized high-frequency rhythmic components, and through occlusion and substitution experiments, the authors identify which speech features (silence, sound intensity, vowels, acoustic onsets) drive retrieval.
AI.motivation: While deep CLIP-style models can retrieve speech from MEG recordings, their weights do not map onto electrophysiological quantities, and it is unclear which speech properties actually drive the retrieval. The authors aim to redesign the architecture so that it is both high-performing and interpretable in neural/anatomical terms.
AI.method: The authors redesign an existing MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture by: (1) replacing flattened sensor-layout spatial attention with spherical harmonics on the 3D MEG helmet geometry; (2) reducing subject-specific branches from 270 to 25, each with a temporal filter to match a neuronal source in space and time; (3) making the convolutional decoder shallower; (4) removing ocular and cardiac components before training. They then perform source mapping, occlusion experiments on stimulus features, substitution with random word lists, and wav2vec dimensionality reduction analyses.
AI.result: The model achieves 39.75 ± 0.34% Top-1 accuracy on MEG-MASC across six trained solutions with ~20x fewer decoder parameters. Weights map to source space recovering speech-perception network generators, with left-lateralized branches carrying higher-frequency rhythmic components. Occlusion shows 15 of 19 stimulus features contribute, with largest effects for silence, sound intensity, vowels, and acoustic onsets. Random word lists behave oppositely—substituting narrative MEG improves retrieval—and wav2vec targets can be reduced to ~12 learned dimensions without accuracy loss, though strong temporal compression degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Source mapping and input interventions reveal that retrieval is driven by specific, anatomically interpretable neural generators and particular acoustic-linguistic features. The architectural redesign makes the model more interpretable while maintaining (even improving) retrieval performance with far fewer parameters, providing insight into what makes speech retrieval from MEG possible.

title: Self-supervised DXA representations encode multi-system disease risk, biological aging and heritability
summary: Whole-body dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans are routinely acquired to measure bone density and regional body composition, leaving their spatial structure largely unused. Here, we show that self-supervised learning (SSL) can convert raw DXA images into representations of systemic health. We introduce LeDXA, a vision model based on a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that learns by predicting latent representations rather than reconstructing pixels. Trained from scratch on 11,540 unlabeled Human Phenotype Project scans, LeDXA was evaluated internally and on 47,400 external UK Biobank (UKBB) scans. It improved cross-cohort prediction of prevalent diseases and biomarkers beyond scanner-derived DXA measurements and DINOv3, a state-of-the-art general-purpose model, despite approximately 150,000-fold fewer training images and nearly 40-fold fewer parameters. Over a median 4.3-year UKBB follow-up, LeDXA improved incident disease prediction over tabular DXA measures, with the largest gains for hip and knee arthrosis and type 2 diabetes. For hip arthrosis, 66% of incident cases occurred in the highest-risk quartile versus 41% for tabular measures. Its representations predicted chronological age externally (r = 0.88; mean absolute error = 2.90 years), and the biological-age gap tracked broader disease burden and a 45% higher mortality hazard in the oldest-appearing quartile. The gap also decreased in women after starting hormone-replacement therapy, suggesting it may be modifiable. Genome-wide associations recovered mostly known body-composition and bone-density loci, and LeDXA embeddings were more heritable than DINOv3's. These findings reveal prognostic information in DXA images that conventional readouts discard, learnable with relatively little data and modest compute.

AI.tldr: LeDXA is a self-supervised vision model (JEPA-based) trained from scratch on just 11,540 unlabeled DXA scans that converts raw dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry images into representations of systemic health. Despite ~150,000x fewer training images and ~40x fewer parameters than DINOv3, it outperforms both tabular DXA measures and DINOv3 on cross-cohort disease/biomarker prediction, incident disease prediction, and biological-age estimation (MAE 2.90 years).
AI.motivation: Whole-body DXA scans are routinely collected for bone density and body composition, but their rich spatial structure remains largely unused. The authors aim to extract latent systemic health information from these ubiquitously available but underutilized imaging data.
AI.method: LeDXA is a vision transformer based on a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), trained via self-supervised learning that predicts latent representations rather than reconstructing pixels. It was trained from scratch on 11,540 unlabeled Human Phenotype Project scans and evaluated internally plus on 47,400 external UK Biobank scans. Performance was benchmarked against tabular DXA measures and DINOv3, and validated through disease prediction, biological-age gap analyses, mortality hazard, and genome-wide association studies.
AI.result: LeDXA improved cross-cohort prediction of prevalent diseases and biomarkers over both tabular DXA measurements and DINOv3 despite far fewer training data and parameters. It improved incident disease prediction (largest gains for hip/knee arthrosis and type 2 diabetes), predicted chronological age externally (r=0.88, MAE=2.90 years), and the biological-age gap tracked disease burden and a 45% higher mortality hazard in the oldest-appearing quartile. The gap decreased after hormone-replacement therapy in women. Embeddings were more heritable than DINOv3's and recovered known body-composition/bone-density loci in GWAS.
AI.conclusion: DXA scans contain substantial prognostic information that conventional readouts discard, and this information is learnable with relatively little data and modest compute via self-supervised learning, revealing broader clinical and biological utility for a widely available imaging modality.
